title: Cipher and Drop
premise: Felix Yarrow, a hostage negotiator who walked away from the job after a botched standoff left a teenager dead, is living quietly under an assumed name when a burner phone arrives with no return address. The voice on the line belongs to Dana Reyes, the negotiator who died in that incident—or someone who knows exactly how she talked, paused, and breathed. The caller forces Felix to negotiate one final crisis: the caller holds proof that the incident was orchestrated by Felix's late mentor, Aldous Wren, whose estate Felix has just inherited, and will release it publicly unless Felix surrenders the encrypted ledger hidden in Wren's papers—a ledger naming every official Wren bought over twenty years. As Felix races corrupt cops and Wren's surviving network to find the ledger first, they discover Dana faked her death to escape Wren's machine and has been hunting its architects ever since; the 'hostage' in this final negotiation is the truth itself. In the climax at the decommissioned call center where the original incident began, Felix chooses loyalty to the dead over self-preservation, broadcasting the ledger live rather than trading it for their own safety, and talks Dana down from killing Wren's last living partner—ending the book with Felix testifying, sleepless but finally free of the board.
about_author: Sebastian Villalobos is a former crisis-line volunteer who spent six years listening to strangers talk themselves back from the edge before turning to fiction. He writes thrillers about people who talk for a living, drawing on his fascination with negotiation as both weapon and confession.

chapters.title: The Number That Shouldn't Exist
chapters.summary: Felix Yarrow's POV. Eighteen months into a quiet life under a new name, Felix works nights at a pawnshop and catalogs insomnia like a hobby. A padded envelope contains a burner phone; when it rings, the voice on the other end recites the exact cadence Felix used in their last failed negotiation. The beat: dread dressed as curiosity—the past knocking politely.

chapters.title: Cadence
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. The caller, identifying herself only as 'the Board,' makes Felix relive the Harrow Street incident in forensic detail, correcting Felix's memory of what was said and when. She demands Felix locate 'the ledger' in mentor Aldous Wren's inherited estate within seven days or she releases recordings proving Wren engineered the incident. Beat: guilt weaponized into a deadline.

chapters.title: Estate Sale
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. Felix returns to Wren's shuttered house for the first time since the funeral, navigating a lifetime of trophies, tapes, and locked drawers while a neighbor reports a break-in. Felix finds a wall safe emptied decades ago except for one index card: a phone number and the word HOLLOWAY. Beat: grief curdling into suspicion of the man who taught them everything.

chapters.title: Detective Okafor
chapters.summary: Detective Adaeze Okafor's POV. Okafor, who caught the pawnshop break-in report, recognizes Felix from the Harrow Street file she's never been allowed to close. She warns Felix that three people connected to the incident have died recently—all ruled accidents. Beat: wary alliance; two insomniacs circling the same wound.

chapters.title: Holloway
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. Following the index card, Felix tracks down Ruth Holloway, Wren's retired dispatcher, now in a care home. Holloway reveals Wren kept a second set of books—payments to judges, captains, councilmen—and that his protégé Dana Reyes found out right before she died. Beat: the failure reframes itself; Dana wasn't collateral, she was a threat.

chapters.title: What the Tape Doesn't Say
chapters.summary: Okafor's POV. Okafor pulls the sealed Harrow Street evidence and notices the negotiation recording has a ninety-second gap precisely where the fatal shot occurs. Her request to reopen the case is denied by a captain whose name appears—she'll later realize—in Wren's orbit. Beat: institutional rot made personal.

chapters.title: Second Caller
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. A second burner activates: a man named Corliss, claiming to represent 'interested parties' who want the ledger destroyed, offering Felix money and a clean exit if they hand over anything they find. When Felix stalls, Corliss mentions the pawnshop's closing time. Beat: pincers closing; invisibility officially over.

chapters.title: The Pawnshop Burns
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. An arson fire destroys the pawnshop and nearly Felix with it; the fire marshal calls it electrical. Felix understands it as a message and goes dark, staying with Okafor against both their better judgments. Beat: survival stripped to essentials; the price of staying silent just became physical.

chapters.title: Dana's Apartment
chapters.summary: Felix and Okafor's alternating POV. They break into Dana Reyes's preserved apartment and find her 'death' was staged—hospital records altered, a closed casket—and a research wall mapping Wren's network, with one node circled in red: CALL CENTER 7, where the incident happened. Beat: hope with teeth; the dead may be hunting too.

chapters.title: Voice Print
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. Comparing the Board's calls to archived tapes of Dana Reyes, Felix confirms the voice is hers—not a mimicry, not grief-driven hallucination. The realization detonates everything Felix believed about that night, including their own role in it. Beat: vertigo; the person Felix failed is alive and furious.

chapters.title: Negotiating With a Ghost
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. Felix finally answers the Board's call by name: 'Dana.' Silence, then fury. Dana lays out her terms plainly—she doesn't want the ledger released piecemeal; she wants Felix to help her take it to a journalist, and she wants Wren's surviving partner, Marcus Vey, delivered to her first. Beat: loyalty vs. truth becomes literal bargaining.

chapters.title: Vey
chapters.summary: Okafor's POV. Okafor investigates Marcus Vey, Wren's fixer turned respected philanthropist, and finds her own captain dining at his foundation gala. She realizes any official channel is compromised and crosses a line, copying files illegally. Beat: the detective becomes the fugitive's ally; institutions fail, people don't have to.

chapters.title: The Ledger Hunt
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. Decoding Wren's habits—his chess notation, his tithing records—Felix deduces the ledger is hidden in plain sight: engraved brass plates lining the memorial bench Wren dedicated after the incident. Digging at night, they retrieve a micro-etched cipher cylinder. Beat: inheritance revealed as trap; the mentor buried his sins in a monument to his victims.

chapters.title: Corliss Closes
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. Corliss intercepts Felix at the memorial park with two men. A brutal, close-quarters escape leaves Felix wounded and Corliss holding Felix's phone—which contains Dana's number. Beat: terror and self-loathing; Felix has just sold out a ghost to save their skin.

chapters.title: Burned Frequency
chapters.summary: Dana's POV (first time). Dana, watching Corliss's crew trace her safehouse, executes a planned disappearance, leaving Felix a single message: 'You had one job. You always do this.' Her chapter reveals her eighteen months hunting the network and why she needed Felix specifically—only a negotiator Wren trained can read the cipher. Beat: betrayal and grudging understanding entwined.

chapters.title: Reading the Dead Man's Hand
chapters.summary: Felix and Okafor's POV. Working from Wren's training materials, Felix cracks the cipher: the ledger names forty-one officials, including the current police commissioner and the judge who sealed the Harrow Street file. It also lists a dead-drop protocol still active—meaning Vey can be lured using Wren's own procedures. Beat: competence restored; the student surpasses the corrupt teacher.

chapters.title: Terms of Surrender
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. Felix contacts Dana through a clean channel and proposes the trade: they'll deliver Vey to Call Center 7, but Dana must let the journalist publish the whole ledger unredacted—including whatever implicates Felix. Dana agrees, and admits the recordings she threatened Felix with were leverage, not vengeance. Mostly. Beat: trust rebuilt on uncomfortable honesty.

chapters.title: Setting the Table
chapters.summary: Okafor's POV. Okafor arranges the lure using Wren's dead-drop protocol, knowing Vey will bring protection and that half the city's power structure wants the ledger gone. She preps extraction routes, gives Felix a wire, and tells them the truth: if this goes wrong, no one is coming. Beat: calm before catastrophe; loyalty chosen with open eyes.

chapters.title: Call Center 7
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. The exchange collapses—Vey arrives knowing everything, Corliss's crew flanks the building, and Dana takes a bullet shielding Felix. Locked inside the decommissioned call center where the incident began, Felix does the only thing they know: starts negotiating, aloud, on an open emergency frequency, narrating everything—names, payments, the gap in the tape—to whoever is listening. Beat: climax ignites; truth as a broadcast weapon.

chapters.title: The Longest Hour
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. Felix negotiates Vey's surrender by dismantling his leverage piece by piece—his men are listening to the broadcast too, and loyalty to a dying conspiracy costs more than cooperation. Corliss stands down when Okafor arrives with the one honest unit she could assemble. Vey, exposed and abandoned, is taken alive. Beat: catharsis through craft; every skill learned from Wren turned against his empire.

chapters.title: Reyes, D.
chapters.summary: Hospital room, Felix and Dana's shared scene. Dana survives; the ledger reaches the journalist intact, and resignations and indictments begin cascading. Dana tells Felix she staged her death because staying visible meant staying owned—and asks Felix what they'll do now that invisible isn't an option either. Beat: mourning and release; two survivors comparing scars.

chapters.title: Sleep
chapters.summary: Felix's POV, epilogue. Months later, Felix testifies at the commission hearings, then visits the Harrow Street memorial—Wren's brass-lined bench, now bearing a new plaque with the victims' real story. That night, back in a small apartment under their own name, Felix sleeps eight hours and wakes to silence: no burner, no board, no debt outstanding. Beat: resolution; the price of survival paid in full, and worth it.
